faq.q: How many times can a 20000mAh power bank charge a phone?
faq.a: In real-world terms (60-70% delivered efficiency), a 20000mAh power bank charges a 5000mAh phone about 2-3 times from empty, or a 4500mAh phone about 2.5-3 times. The advertised 20000mAh is the internal cell capacity at 3.7V; what reaches your phone at 5V is about 13,000-14,000mAh. If you see a '20000mAh' power bank advertised with a phone-charge count of 6-8, the marketing is wrong or the cells are mislabelled.

faq.q: Is 65W PD enough for a laptop?
faq.a: Yes for most 13-inch laptops (MacBook Air, Dell XPS 13, HP EliteBook) and thin-and-light 14-inch laptops. 65W charges a MacBook Air at full speed (Apple's official charger is 30W-35W for the Air, so 65W gives plenty of headroom). For 15-16 inch performance laptops (MacBook Pro 16, Dell XPS 15, gaming laptops), you need 100W+ PD 3.1 -- which is why the Anker 737 (140W) is the right pick for those.

faq.q: Can I take a 20000mAh power bank on a flight?
faq.a: Yes. Indian airline rules follow the international IATA standard: power banks under 100Wh are allowed in cabin baggage, power banks 100-160Wh need airline approval, and power banks over 160Wh are banned from all flights. A 20000mAh power bank at 3.7V nominal is 74Wh -- well under the 100Wh limit and allowed in cabin baggage without airline approval. Power banks are NOT allowed in checked baggage under any circumstance (lithium-ion fire risk in cargo hold).

faq.q: What is BIS certification and why does it matter?
faq.a: BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) certification is mandatory for lithium-ion power banks sold in India under the 2020-2021 electronics safety rules. A BIS-certified power bank has passed thermal runaway, short-circuit, and overcharge tests at a certified Indian lab. Uncertified power banks are confiscated at airport security, and they have a higher risk of thermal runaway (catching fire) during overcharge or short-circuit. Always look for the 'BIS' mark or 'ISI' mark on the power bank body or packaging.

faq.q: Should I charge my phone with 65W or 18W?
faq.a: Modern phones support between 18W (older Pixel 6, older Samsung) and 100W+ (latest OnePlus, latest Xiaomi flagships). For most phones in 2026, 30W-65W is enough to charge from 0-100% in about 45-60 minutes. Charging with 18W works fine but takes 90-120 minutes. The phone will only pull as much as its charging circuit requests -- so a 65W power bank doesn't damage a 18W phone, it just delivers at 18W.

body:
What actually matters in a power bank

A power bank is one of the most-purchased phone accessories in India, and the 2026 lineup has stratified enough that the wrong choice is usually picking a no-BIS unmarked brick or an 18W QC3.0 unit when the phone supports 30W-65W USB-C PD. In 2026, the categories have stratified by real capacity (the marketed number vs what actually reaches your phone), output protocol (QC3.0 vs USB-C PD vs PD 3.1), and certification (BIS-certified vs unmarked marketplace listings).

The four things that actually move the needle on an Indian power bank in 2026 are real capacity, output protocol, BIS certification, and airline compliance. Brand matters too, but the four major brands in this list (Ambrane, Mi, Anker, Realme) all have reachable customer service -- the gap is in protocol support and certification.

If you only buy one thing from this list: the Ambrane Stylo 20000mAh 65W PD Power Bank. It has 20000mAh real capacity, 65W USB-C PD output (charges a MacBook Air at full speed), BIS-certified lithium-ion cells, and is airline-approved under the 100Wh cabin-luggage limit.

Capacity: 20000mAh is the sweet-spot for most Indian buyers

A 10000mAh power bank charges a 5000mAh phone once and is borderline for a full day's travel use. A 30000mAh power bank is overkill for daily carry and crosses the 100Wh airline cabin-luggage threshold (a 30000mAh bank at 3.7V is 111Wh -- requires airline approval). The 20000mAh class is the sweet-spot: charges a phone 2-3 times, fits in a backpack, and stays under the 100Wh airline limit (20000mAh at 3.7V is 74Wh).

Output protocol: USB-C PD is the new default

USB-C Power Delivery (PD) is the new standard. Modern phones (iPhone 15+, Pixel 6+, Samsung Galaxy S22+, OnePlus 9+) support 25W-100W PD over USB-C. Older protocols like Qualcomm Quick Charge 3.0 (QC3.0) cap at 18W and don't work with laptops. For 2026 Indian buyers, 30W-65W PD is the right output range -- enough for phones and most 13-inch laptops, but not expensive overkill.

BIS certification: mandatory for airline travel and safety

BIS (Bureau of Indian Standards) certification has been mandatory for lithium-ion power banks sold in India since 2020-2021. A BIS-certified power bank has passed thermal runaway, short-circuit, and overcharge tests at a certified Indian lab. Uncertified marketplace listings are confiscated at airport security and have a higher risk of thermal runaway (catching fire) during overcharge or short-circuit. Always look for the 'BIS' or 'ISI' mark on the power bank body or packaging.

Airline compliance: 74Wh is the magic number

Indian airline rules follow the international IATA standard: power banks under 100Wh are allowed in cabin baggage without approval, power banks 100-160Wh need airline approval, and power banks over 160Wh are banned from all flights. A 20000mAh power bank at 3.7V nominal is 74Wh -- well under the 100Wh limit and allowed in cabin baggage. Power banks are NOT allowed in checked baggage under any circumstance (lithium-ion fire risk in cargo hold). Carry your power bank in your hand-luggage only.

The 65W USB-C PD output charges a MacBook Air at full speed and modern phones at 45W-65W. The BIS-certified lithium-ion cells pass Indian safety standards and are airline-approved under 100Wh cabin-luggage limits.

Capacity8000-10000mAh claim
Output10W no-PD
Cert.Often no BIS

The sub-Rs 800 power bank listings promise 10000-20000mAh with no protocol support and no BIS certification. The reality is 8000-10000mAh at best, with unmarked lithium-ion cells that fail thermal-runaway tests. These are confiscated at airport security, and they have a documented history of catching fire during overcharge or short-circuit.

We also recommend skipping any power bank without a visible BIS/ISI mark on the body or packaging. The price difference between a sub-Rs 800 power bank and the Ambrane Capsule (Rs 1,200-1,600) is Rs 400-800 -- which is the cost of replacing the cheap power bank once. The Ambrane lasts 2-3 years; the cheap power bank lasts 3-8 months.

The bottom line

Buy the Ambrane Stylo 20000mAh 65W PD if you want the most balanced 20000mAh power bank in India with 65W USB-C PD output at the lowest price. For a tighter budget without laptop charging, the Mi Power Bank 3i 20000mAh is a credible 18W QC3.0 alternative at a lower price. The Anker 737 GaNPrime 140W is the right pick if you need to charge a performance laptop at full speed.

For buyers who want USB-C PD at a price lower than the Ambrane Stylo, the Realme 20000mAh 30W is the right mid-budget pick. The Ambrane 10000mAh 22.5W Capsule is the pocketable everyday-carry under Rs 1,500. Whatever you pick, look for the BIS mark on the body or packaging, and remember to carry it in your cabin baggage on flights -- never check it.
